analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to buy goods and services from private contractors instead of doing work in-house.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with 24 House Republican backers and never received a markup, hearing, or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made outside contractors the default provider for nearly everything federal agencies need. Agencies would have to buy goods and services from private sources unless the agency head certified an exemption — for work required by law, national defense or homeland security, inherently governmental functions, or when no private source exists. It also required an annual government study and a five-year schedule for transferring commercial work to contractors.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal contractors, government-services firms, and outsourcing companies would gain a government-guaranteed market, since agencies would be required to procure from private sources unless they certified an exemption. The bill's sponsors argued taxpayers benefit because private companies are more efficient competitors than the government itself.

how_it_helps.text: Each executive department, military department, and independent establishment would be required to obtain all goods and services needed for its functions by procurement from private sources.

Agencies could keep work in-house only through narrow exemptions: work required by law, a certified finding that the work is necessary for national defense or homeland security, work so inherently governmental it must stay with federal employees, or cases where no private source can provide it.

Private provision would happen through divestiture of federal involvement, competitively awarded contracts, or a public-private competitive sourcing analysis finding that private provision is in the government's best interest and the best value to the taxpayer.

The Office of Management and Budget, with the Comptroller General, would have to report annually on each agency's activities and include a schedule to transfer commercial activities to the private sector within five years.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would pay for the contracts, including contractor profit margins and overhead. Federal employees could lose work or jobs as commercial activities are transferred to the private sector on the bill's five-year schedule, and agencies would face the cost of annual studies, certifications, and sourcing analyses.

drawbacks.text: Private procurement would be the default for all work 'necessary for or beneficial to' agency functions; keeping work with federal employees would require passing an OMB-based competitive sourcing analysis and a best-value determination, so the cheaper option has to prove itself rather than being the starting point.

The exemptions require an agency head to determine and certify them under OMB regulations — not a comparison of in-house versus contractor cost — so an agency could not simply choose federal employees because they cost less.
States and localities would have had to comply with the private-procurement policy when spending federal funds, extending the mandate beyond federal agencies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Competitive sourcing can produce savings in some cases, and the bill's backers point to its own process for determining best value. But the structure presumes the answer: private contractors are the default, and in-house work survives only through exemptions and analyses. Outsourcing typically adds contractor profit and overhead, and shifting inherently public work to companies can reduce accountability. On balance the bill would mainly have transferred government work and public money to contractors, with savings possible but not guaranteed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee the day it was introduced and never received a committee markup or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 28, 2015, by Rep. John Duncan Jr. of Tennessee and referred the same day to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the bill's action history.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, so the bill expired without ever leaving committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal contractors did not gain a government-mandated market, and federal employees kept the default role of performing agency work in-house; taxpayers avoided a large new outsourcing program, though no competitive-sourcing savings were pursued either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Contractors lost a windfall; federal work stayed in-house

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 28, 2015 and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Jason Chaffetz
against.role: Chair, House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or sent it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 supporters — the sponsor and 23 cosponsors — were House Republicans, and the bill died in a committee controlled by a Republican chair without a vote.

industries.note: The bill would make private procurement the default channel for nearly all agency goods and services, creating a permanent, government-guaranteed market for contractors. Keeping work in-house would require exemptions or passing a sourcing analysis, so the potentially cheaper public alternative would no longer be the starting point.

Federal employees could lose work or jobs as commercial activities are transferred to private providers on a five-year schedule. Their interest in keeping work in-house runs alongside the public interest in accountable, potentially lower-cost government service.

States and localities would have had to follow the private-procurement policy when spending federal funds, restricting their own in-house operations. This reduces their flexibility in how they deliver services to residents.
